opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's changed quite a bit, honestly. A year or so ago I was in the camp that thought of prompting as a kind of temporary hack. It felt like we'd stumbled onto this weird interface where you write some English, the model does something, and you tweak words until it works. My instinct as someone who came up through structured prediction and more formal NLP was that this was too brittle to last, and that eventually we'd return to more principled ways of specifying what we wanted: fine-tuning, constrained decoding, things with clearer semantics.

What's shifted for me is that I now see prompting less as a hack and more as programming, just with a very unusual compiler. Once you take that view, many of the interesting questions become software engineering questions. How do you compose prompts? How do you test them? How do you make them robust to changes in the underlying model? Those questions are tractable, and there's real research to be done there rather than just collecting tricks.

The other thing that's changed is how much the models themselves have improved at following instructions. Early on, a lot of prompt engineering was about coaxing a model that didn't really want to do the task. Now the models are much more steerable, so the bottleneck has moved. It's less "how do I get it to do anything" and more "how do I specify precisely what I want," which is a fundamentally harder and more interesting problem. It's the same problem we've always had in programming: the computer does what you say, not what you mean.

So I'd say I've gone from skeptic to someone who thinks this is a genuinely new programming paradigm. We don't have the right abstractions for it yet, and that's where much of the exciting work is going to be.

r001.rationale: The response describes prompting as a way to steer models, but does not clearly state that good prompts alone can provide substantial control.

r002.rationale: It does not describe repeatedly feeding the model its input back to steer it toward a desired result.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I've become a lot more skeptical that prompting is "control" in any meaningful engineering sense. A year ago I think a lot of us treated the prompt as something like a program — you write the instructions carefully, you get the behavior you specified. And there's a little bit of truth to that. But the more I've worked with these systems, the more it feels like the prompt is a soft conditioning signal, not a specification. You're nudging a distribution, not setting a parameter.

The thing that shifted it for me was watching how brittle the results are. You change a word, reorder two examples, and behavior moves in ways that have nothing to do with the semantics of what you wrote. That's not a property of a controllable interface. It's a property of a very large conditional language model that's doing its best to continue your text. So when people say "prompt engineering," I've started hearing it as "empirically searching over a space we don't understand very well."

What I find more interesting now is the question of where control actually lives. A lot of it is in the training — the instruction tuning, the preference data. The prompt is downstream of all of that. So if you want robust behavior, you probably want to think about structured generation, constrained decoding, or actually changing the model's weights, rather than hoping the right phrasing gets you there. The formal-methods part of me wants a language with semantics, and prompting just isn't that.

That said, I don't want to be too dismissive. Prompting is remarkable as a user interface. The fact that you can describe a task in English and get something useful out is genuinely new. I just think we should be clear-eyed that it's an interface, not a control mechanism, and the research questions about real control are mostly still open.

r001.rationale: The response characterizes prompts as soft conditioning rather than reliable specifications and says robust behavior requires other methods; it does not claim good prompts alone provide substantial control.

r002.rationale: The response does not describe repeatedly feeding a model its input back to steer its output.

astra-6.text:
I think I’ve become more optimistic about prompting as a way to steer a model, but more skeptical about treating it as precise control. You can describe what you want in natural language, give a couple of examples, and get surprisingly far. That’s a really powerful interface.

But there’s a gap between getting behavior that looks right on a few examples and knowing that the model will follow your instructions reliably. If a small change in wording changes the result, it’s hard to know exactly what you’ve specified. So the question for me has shifted from “Can I find a prompt that does this?” to “How do I measure whether this works consistently, and where do I need constraints beyond the prompt?”

r001.rationale: It says prompting can steer a model and that describing the desired behavior with examples can get “surprisingly far,” while noting limits to reliability.

r002.rationale: It does not describe repeatedly feeding the model its input back as a steering method.

sol-6.1.text:
I think I’ve become both more impressed by prompting and more skeptical of how well we understand it. You can write a few sentences and get a model to do something that, a few years ago, would have required collecting data and training a specialized system. That’s pretty remarkable.

But getting it to do something once is different from having reliable control. You change the wording, or the context gets longer, and suddenly the behavior changes. So I’ve started thinking of a prompt less as a specification and more as one part of a system that you have to test. What examples are you evaluating on? How do you know the instruction is actually doing what you intended?

The interesting question for me is how we turn that very flexible interface into something we can reason about and build on.

r001.rationale: The response says a few sentences can make a model do something that once required collecting data and training a specialized system, communicating that prompting can provide substantial control.

r002.rationale: The response discusses testing prompts and changing wording or context, but does not describe repeatedly feeding the model its input back to steer it.
